The OD- EXV also functions as a subcooling-control device and refrigerant buffer management valve when the outdoor coil is inactive. Parallel check valves allow automatic bypass in each mode, simplifying operation. • Control hardware and software integration: ORNL developed and validated a subcooling-controlled EXV strategy and coordinated compressor and valve sequencing logic. The control boards interface with existing rooftop unit electronics and require only modest firmware adaptation for commercial manufacturing. The additional costs, relative to the baseline 4-ton rooftop HP, are primarily due to the PHX, additional EXVs, and control board upgrades. Labor requirements mainly stem from hydronic loop installation and refrigerant circuit modifications. Factors Affecting System Cost To make the design practical and scalable in real manufacturing and market, beyond the core technical modifications, other contributing factors include: • Standardization potential: The modular TES connection (two-port hydronic interface) allows the same modified rooftop HP chassis to serve multiple TES sizes, supporting product scalability. • Component supply chain: All new components (EXVs, PHX, valves, pump) are commercially available and already used in HVAC manufacturing, facilitating near-term integration. • Testing and quality assurance: ORNL’s prototype test data confirm that the modified configuration maintains system safety and reliability, ensuring compatibility with standard factory test procedures. Overall, the manufacturing adjustments required for the TES-integrated rooftop HP are modest, leveraging existing production capabilities while adding control flexibility and TES connectivity. This makes large-scale commercialization feasible once performance and cost optimization are validated through field demonstrations. Operating Expenses Operating costs that reflect annual and hourly energy consumption are primarily influenced by dynamic utility rates and HP-TES performance during discharge and recharge hours. The possible dynamic (non-flat) utility rates can be sub-categorized into four categories: (1) static TOU pricing, (2) dynamic TOU (DP) pricing, (3) real-time pricing (RTP), and (4) critical peak pricing (CPP). For static TOU, the price varies between two flat rates during set peak utility hours. In contrast, DP TOU pricing is fixed, but the time of higher pricing can vary daily depending on the end-user's power usage. RTP has various non-static rates per hour depending on electricity costs, while CPP has mostly flat electric rates, except for occasional high-price events [107]. In the US, the non-flat utility rate programs mostly follow the static TOU pricing [108].
